title: Digital Omnibus on AI — Proposal amending Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (COM(2025) 836 final) and the 2026 co-legislator agreement postponing high-risk obligations
pub: European Commission (COM(2025) 836 final, 19 November 2025); EPRS briefing PE 782.651 (July 2026)
author: European Commission · European Parliamentary Research Service

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess jagged legal-task capability, human verification or redesign of legal workflows. It instead reframes selective deployment as a regulatory-readiness problem, advocating delayed obligations, compliance support, sandboxes and centralised oversight while preserving substantive protections.
qs: These include delays in designating national competent authorities and conformity assessment bodies, as well as a lack of harmonised standards for the AI Act’s high-risk requirements, guidance, and compliance tools.

st.t: EU governance: Simplification tests enforceable safeguards
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core balance between workable simplification and enforceable protection, then materially develops it by tracing implementation delays, negotiated timetable changes, burden reductions, restored safeguards and stakeholder disputes. It also appropriately treats claimed benefits and harms as proposals or attributed views rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: Its purpose is to promote innovation and the uptake of AI while ensuring a high level of protection for health, safety, and fundamental rights, including democracy and the rule of law.

The co-legislators reinstated a simplified registration obligation for non-high-risk AI systems, and the strict-necessity standard for processing special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction.

kp.d: The Commission attributes implementation difficulties to delayed national authorities and conformity assessment bodies and missing standards, guidance and compliance tools. It argues these deficiencies could increase compliance costs and slow innovation, presenting simplification as compatible with maintaining health, safety and fundamental-rights protections. These are regulatory claims concerning AI generally, rather than findings about legal-profession restructuring.
qs: These include delays in designating national competent authorities and conformity assessment bodies, as well as a lack of harmonised standards for the AI Act’s high-risk requirements, guidance, and compliance tools.
Such delays risk significantly increasing the compliance costs for businesses and public authorities and slowing down innovation.

kp.k: Agreement replaces conditional postponement with fixed high-risk deadlines
kp.d: The November 2025 proposal would trigger high-risk obligations six months after a Commission compliance-support decision for Annex III systems and 12 months afterwards for Annex I systems, subject to final deadlines. EPRS reports that the 7 May 2026 trilogue instead agreed fixed dates: 2 December 2027 for stand-alone high-risk systems and 2 August 2028 for high-risk systems embedded in products. EPRS reports Parliament's approval on 16 June 2026; the supplied material does not establish Official Journal publication of the agreed amendment.
qs: The co-legislators reached a trilogue agreement on 7 May 2026.

They agreed to prohibit AI practices generating non-consensual intimate or sexual content and child sexual abuse material, and to set fixed deadlines for the delayed application of high-risk AI rules: 2 December 2027 for stand-alone high-risk AI systems, and 2 August 2028 for high-risk AI systems embedded in products.

kp.k: AI literacy proposal shifts responsibility toward public encouragement
kp.d: The Commission proposes replacing the horizontal obligation on providers and deployers to ensure staff AI literacy with an obligation on the Commission and Member States to encourage it, while retaining training obligations for high-risk deployers. Its rationale is that a uniform obligation is ineffective and burdens smaller enterprises. EPRS reports Parliament's preference that providers and deployers support staff literacy, but its trilogue summary does not specify the final literacy provision.
qs: requiring the Commission and the Member States to foster AI literacy instead enforcing unspecified obligation on providers and deployers of AI systems in this respect, while training obligations for high-risk deployers remain;

Moreover, data indicate that imposing such an obligation creates an additional compliance burden, particularly for smaller enterprises, whereas AI literacy should be a strategic priority, regardless of regulatory obligations and potential sanctions.

kp.k: Agreement restores registration and strict sensitive-data necessity
kp.d: The proposal removes EU database registration for Annex III systems assessed as non-high-risk, but retains documentation of that assessment and disclosure to national authorities on request. It also expands exceptional processing of special-category personal data for bias detection and correction to additional providers, deployers and models, subject to safeguards. EPRS reports that the agreement reinstated simplified registration and the strict-necessity standard, distinguishing the compromise from the Commission's original approach.
qs: A provider who considers that an AI system referred to in Annex III is not high-risk shall document its assessment before that system is placed on the market or put into service.

The co-legislators reinstated a simplified registration obligation for non-high-risk AI systems, and the strict-necessity standard for processing special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction.

kp.k: Centralised AI Office supervision requires additional specialised capacity
kp.d: The proposal gives the AI Office exclusive supervision of systems based on general-purpose models developed by the same provider, excluding Annex I product-related systems, and systems constituting or integrated into designated very large platforms or search engines. The Commission predicts more consistent enforcement and less regulatory duplication. It estimates 53 FTE for the new tasks, comprising 15 redeployed and 38 additional FTE. EPRS reports reinforced AI Office powers in the agreement without reproducing their complete final scope.
qs: The AI Office shall also be exclusively competent for the supervision and enforcement of the obligations under this Regulation in relation to AI system that constitute or that are integrated into a designated very large online platform or very large online search engine within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065.
New resources will be needed (estimated in 38 additional FTEs) to efficiently exercise the new enforcement tasks.
The enforcement of the new regulation is estimated to require 53 FTE.

kp.k: Smaller enterprises receive broader compliance accommodations
kp.d: The Commission proposes extending simplified technical documentation, size-sensitive quality management and penalty accommodations from SMEs to small mid-caps. Separately, simplified compliance with certain quality-management elements would expand from microenterprises to all SMEs. These accommodations are not presented as exemptions from substantive high-risk protections. EPRS reports that the agreement extended simplified documentation to medium-sized companies.
qs: SMCs and SMEs, including start-ups, may provide the elements of the technical documentation specified in Annex IV in a simplified manner.
Providers shall, in any event, respect the degree of rigour and the level of protection required to ensure the compliance of their high-risk AI systems with this Regulation.
They extended the simplified documentation process for medium-sized companies, and reinforced the AI Office's powers.

kp.k: Sandboxes and real-world testing expand supervised experimentation
kp.d: The proposal enables an EU-level sandbox for systems within the AI Office's competence, with priority access for SMEs, and strengthens cross-border cooperation between national sandboxes. It extends real-world testing outside sandboxes to Section A Annex I product-related high-risk systems and introduces voluntary Commission–Member State agreements for Section B systems. The financial statement anticipates an operational EU sandbox in 2028, rather than reporting an existing facility.
qs: The first EU sandbox is expected to be operational in 2028, although some key setting details should be established beforehand.

Such an AI regulatory sandbox shall be implemented in close cooperation with relevant competent authorities, in particular when Union legislation other than this Regulation is supervised in the AI regulatory sandbox, and shall provide priority access to SMEs.
The voluntary real-world testing agreement referred to in paragraph 1 shall be concluded in writing between interested Member States and the Commission.

kp.k: Machinery moves toward sectoral rather than direct AI regulation
kp.d: EPRS reports that the agreement removes AI-enabled machinery from direct application of the AI Act's high-risk regime, relying instead on the Machinery Regulation. The Commission must adopt delegated acts incorporating relevant AI health and safety requirements into that regulation. Reported stakeholder reactions distinguish machinery from medical devices and toys, which remain in the AI Act; industry and consumer groups disagree over whether sectoral treatment simplifies compliance or weakens safeguards.
qs: They removed AI- enabled machinery products from the direct applicability of the AI Act's high-risk regime, clarifying that they need only comply with the sectoral approach in the Machinery Regulation.

The Commission is required to adopt delegated acts amending Annex III of the Machinery Regulation in order to include health and safety requirements relating to AI systems that are classified as high-risk and that are either safety components in machinery or machinery themselves.

kp.k: Agreement changes marking deadlines and adds prohibited practices
kp.d: The Commission proposed allowing systems generating synthetic audio, images, video or text already marketed before 2 August 2026 until 2 February 2027 to meet Article 50(2) marking requirements. EPRS reports the agreement instead sets 2 December 2026 for these existing systems and adds prohibitions concerning non-consensual intimate or sexual content and child sexual abuse material. The marking postponement is therefore distinct from the high-risk implementation postponement.
qs: The obligation to mark AI-generated content was delayed to 2 December 2026 for systems on the market before 2 August 2026.

They agreed to prohibit AI practices generating non-consensual intimate or sexual content and child sexual abuse material, and to set fixed deadlines for the delayed application of high-risk AI rules: 2 December 2027 for stand-alone high-risk AI systems, and 2 August 2028 for high-risk AI systems embedded in products.

kp.k: Compliance streamlining retains documentation and monitoring duties
kp.d: The proposal provides a single application and assessment route for conformity assessment bodies where relevant sectoral legislation permits it, intended to avoid duplication while maintaining both sets of requirements. It removes the prescribed harmonised post-market monitoring template, not the obligation to maintain a monitoring plan, and requires Commission guidance instead. These changes concern the organisation of compliance work rather than eliminating substantive oversight.
qs: The single application and single assessment procedure shall avoid any unnecessary duplications, build on the existing procedures for designation under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I and ensure compliance with the requirements both relating to notified bodies under this Regulation and the relevant Union harmonisation legislation.
The post-market monitoring system shall be based on a post-market monitoring plan.
The Commission shall adopt guidance on the post-market monitoring plan.

kp.k: Savings estimates are prospective and differ between supplied texts
kp.d: The Commission memorandum projects possible savings of approximately EUR 297.2–433.2 million, while EPRS reports up to €429.5 million in annual administrative savings. EPRS attributes €222.75 million to changing AI literacy obligations, €68 million–€204 million to postponing high-risk rules, and €2.5 million to extending the SME regime to small mid-caps. These are estimates for proposed changes, not measured savings or demonstrated impacts of the final agreement. The Commission did not conduct a separate impact assessment, arguing that the amendments were technical.
qs: Initial estimates project possible savings of ≈ EUR 297.2 to 433.2 million.
According to Commission estimates, the proposed amendments to the AI Act could save up to €429.5 million in administrative costs per year.
The largest cost savings would result from transforming the obligation of AI literacy under the AI Act, which would enable businesses to save €222.75 million.
There are no policy options that could meaningfully be tested and compared in an impact assessment report.

kp.k: Stakeholders contest simplification's effects on innovation and rights
kp.d: EPRS describes divergent views rather than a settled finding: industry groups generally support simplification and postponement, whereas civil society and consumer organisations criticise weakened transparency and delayed protection. The EDPB and EDPS support addressing implementation challenges but seek strict sensitive-data limits and oppose removing registration and changing literacy obligations. Consultation evidence includes 718 responses across three initial consultations, 513 responses to the September–October 2025 call for evidence and 106 SME-panel responses; these are consultation counts, not causal evidence of regulatory effects.
qs: Stakeholder and academic views on the Digital Omnibus on AI diverge sharply.

However, the joint opinion calls for strict limits when allowing the use of special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction and opposes deleting registration requirements and changes to AI literacy.
Taken together, 718 responses were received as part of this first consultation exercise.
A total of 513 responses were received, by a wide range of stakeholders.

kp.k: Agentic AI creates distinct supervisory challenges
kp.d: The Commission's financial statement identifies autonomous operation and consequential decisions as particular challenges for AI Office supervision and calls for strategies to address them. The proposed notified-body classification separately lists agentic AI as AIH 0401. This is a regulatory planning claim, not empirical evidence of agent deployment or resulting changes in legal employment.
qs: The AI Office will also need to consider the unique challenges posed by agentic AI, which can operate autonomously and make decisions that may have significant consequences, and develop strategies to address these risks in line with Commission policies.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: This cross-domain source makes claims about AI regulation, compliance costs, innovation, oversight and public protection, rather than lawyer productivity, law-firm staffing or legal-service markets.
pts.d: The Commission claims that delayed standards, guidance, competent authorities and conformity assessment arrangements create heavier-than-expected compliance burdens and risk slowing innovation. It predicts that targeted simplification will make AI Act implementation more predictable and innovation-friendly. Its proposed mechanisms include delaying high-risk obligations, replacing the horizontal staff AI-literacy obligation with public encouragement, extending selected SME privileges to small mid-caps, simplifying conformity-assessment procedures, removing registration for certain systems assessed as non-high-risk, and allowing greater flexibility in post-market monitoring. The Commission projects possible administrative savings of approximately EUR 297.2–433.2 million in its memorandum; EPRS separately reports Commission estimates of up to EUR 429.5 million annually, including EUR 222.75 million from AI-literacy changes, EUR 68–204 million from timing changes and EUR 2.5 million from extending the SME regime. These are projections, not realised savings, and the supplied text does not reconcile the different totals. The Commission further predicts that centralised AI Office supervision will reduce conflicting interpretations, regulatory duplication and national staffing burdens, while concentrating specialist expertise. Expanded sandboxes and real-world testing are intended to accelerate market access and innovation. It characterises bias detection and correction as protecting people against discrimination, including outside high-risk systems, and recognises autonomous agentic AI as posing potentially consequential risks. Its claim that simplification will not lower fundamental-rights protection is contested in the stakeholder accounts reported by EPRS, rather than established as a shared conclusion. EPRS also reports the legislative agreement's concrete changes, including fixed high-risk deadlines, restored simplified registration and strict necessity for sensitive-data processing, and a sectoral machinery regime.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The basis is Commission internal analysis, stakeholder implementation experience, consultation responses, prior impact assessments and institutional reporting; the text does not present measured post-reform outcomes.
pts.d: For implementation difficulties and expected simplification benefits, the Commission cites existing data, written feedback, a reality check and consultations summarised in its accompanying staff working document. It reports 718 responses across three spring/summer 2025 consultations on the broader digital package, 513 responses to the September–October call for evidence and 106 SME-panel responses. These are consultation counts, not representative measures of AI adoption or causal estimates of regulatory effects. The Commission says it mainly relied on internal analysis and did not undertake a separate impact assessment because it regarded the amendments as technical and not amenable to meaningful comparison of policy options. The supplied document gives headline savings estimates but not their full calculations. Its governance predictions draw partly on experience enforcing the Digital Services Act, including cooperation with national authorities and action against platforms, without quantified comparative outcomes. EPRS provides an institutional account of the legislative process and an explicitly non-exhaustive overview of divergent views. Industry support, civil-society concerns and academic arguments are attributed positions, not EPRS findings that the predicted benefits or harms will occur. For example, Karin Väyrynen and colleagues argue that the Act provides guardrails enabling trustworthy innovation; Kamrul Faisal warns that simplification risks weakening safeguards; TIC Council warns that sector-specific regimes could increase complexity. These positions should not be attributed to the Commission or adopted as the briefing author's own conclusions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Distinguish the Commission's conditional November 2025 proposal from the fixed deadlines in the 2026 agreement reported by EPRS.
pts.d: The Commission proposal dated 19 November 2025 would make high-risk obligations apply six months after a Commission decision confirming adequate compliance support for Annex III systems and twelve months after that decision for Annex I systems, subject to backstop dates of 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028 respectively. EPRS reports that the 7 May 2026 trilogue agreement instead adopted these as fixed deadlines for stand-alone high-risk systems and high-risk systems embedded in products; Parliament approved the agreement on 16 June 2026. The supplied account does not establish Official Journal publication or entry into force of the amendment, so the agreement should not be conflated with an already operative regulation. The Commission proposed a 2 February 2027 marking deadline for generative systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026; EPRS reports an agreed deadline of 2 December 2026 for that cohort. The proposed EU-level sandbox is expected to become operational in 2028, with strengthened provisions reviewed alongside the AI Act in August 2029. Proposal-level grandfathering would cover existing high-risk systems unless significantly changed, with a 2 August 2030 compliance deadline for systems intended for public-authority use. Other qualifications matter: high-risk deployer training remains despite the proposed horizontal AI-literacy change; non-high-risk classification remains documented even under the proposed removal of registration; sensitive-data processing is exceptional and safeguarded, with strict necessity restored in the reported agreement; centralised supervision applies to specified categories rather than all AI. The agreement summary does not establish the final wording of every original proposal, including the AI-literacy provision. Savings forecasts attach to proposed changes and should not automatically be transferred to the modified agreement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects concern AI providers and deployers, smaller enterprises, regulators, conformity-assessment bodies and people exposed to AI systems.
pts.d: Providers and deployers are expected to gain preparation time, lower administrative costs and clearer compliance routes. SMEs, start-ups and small mid-caps are singled out as disproportionately burdened; selected documentation and penalty privileges extend to small mid-caps, while simplified quality-management compliance expands from microenterprises to SMEs. Conformity-assessment bodies would gain a single application and assessment route where relevant sectoral law permits. Providers within specified general-purpose-model and very-large-platform/search-engine categories would face central AI Office supervision, while product-related and other exceptions limit that scope. The Commission estimates 53 FTE for new tasks, comprising 15 redeployed and 38 additional personnel; it specifically identifies legal and procedural expertise for enforcement work, but makes no wider prediction about legal employment. National authorities are expected to be relieved of some oversight burdens, while fundamental-rights authorities gain clarified information-access and cooperation arrangements. Product sectors face differentiated treatment: EPRS reports machinery moving to a sectoral approach, with medical devices and toys remaining within the AI Act. Staff and other AI operators are affected by changes to literacy obligations. Data subjects may benefit from bias correction but are also exposed to sensitive-data processing; the public is affected by the timing and strength of transparency, high-risk safeguards and prohibitions. EPRS reports that consumer and civil-society groups fear weaker or delayed protection, whereas industry groups generally anticipate improved implementation and competitiveness. No source-specific conclusion is offered about law firms, ALSPs, legal departments, legal fees or access to justice.
